# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Modern Perspective on Diagnosis and Therapy

### Introduction
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive, life-threatening infiltrative cardiomyopathy characterized by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium [1]. Historically considered a rare disease, recent advances in non-invasive imaging have demonstrated that CA is a major underdiagnosed cause of heart failure, particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and severe aortic stenosis [2]. The two primary types of amyloid proteins that infiltrate the myocardium are monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (AL amyloidosis) and transthyretin (ATTR amyloidosis) [3]. ATTR amyloidosis is further categorized into a hereditary form (ATTRv, variant) caused by genetic mutations, and a wild-type form (ATTRwt) associated with aging [4].

### Pathophysiology
The pathophysiology of CA varies significantly by subtype. In AL amyloidosis, a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia produces unstable, cardiotoxic free light chains that rapidly form amyloid fibrils [5]. In contrast, ATTR amyloidosis involves the destabilization of the transthyretin homotetramer, synthesized primarily by the liver, into unstable monomers that misfold and aggregate [6]. These fibrils disrupt the extracellular matrix, leading to progressive myocardial stiffness, diastolic dysfunction, and eventually restrictive cardiomyopathy [7]. Concurrently, the direct toxic effect of circulating light chains in AL amyloidosis can cause rapid, severe cardiomyocyte damage, explaining the more acute clinical course compared to ATTR [8].

### Clinical Red Flags and Diagnosis
Early diagnosis of CA remains a critical challenge due to non-specific initial symptoms. However, several clinical "red flags" should alert the clinician. These include bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, ruptured biceps tendon, and autonomic dysfunction, which often precede cardiac manifestations by several years [9]. Electrocardiography (ECG) may reveal low QRS voltage [10], although pseudo-infarction patterns or left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) are also common [11]. Echocardiography typically demonstrates concentric LV thickening with a characteristic "granular sparkling" appearance, biatrial enlargement [12], and decreased longitudinal strain with "apical sparing" [13].

The diagnostic paradigm of CA has shifted dramatically with the advent of advanced cardiovascular imaging. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides high-resolution tissue characterization [14]. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) typically reveals a diffuse, subendocardial, or transmural pattern, while T1 mapping and extracellular volume (ECV) quantification serve as sensitive markers for early-stage disease and disease burden [15].

Crucially, nuclear scintigraphy using bone-seeking radiotracers, such as technetium-99m pyrophosphate ($^{99m}\text{Tc}$-PYP) or $^{99m}\text{Tc}$-3,3-diphosphono-1,2-propanodicarboxylic acid ($^{99m}\text{Tc}$-DPD), allows for the non-invasive diagnosis of ATTR CA [16]. A Grade 2 or 3 myocardial uptake on planar or SPECT imaging, in the absolute absence of a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia, is diagnostic of ATTR CA with nearly 100% specificity, eliminating the need for invasive endomyocardial biopsy in many patients [17]. To safely apply this non-invasive algorithm, clinicians must rigorously rule out AL amyloidosis using serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis and serum free light chain (FLC) assays [18]. If a monoclonal protein is detected, or if imaging results are equivocal, an endomyocardial or extracardiac biopsy remains mandatory to confirm the diagnosis and perform mass spectrometry or immunohistochemical typing [19,20].

### Management Strategies
The therapeutic landscape for CA has undergone a revolutionary transformation, transitioning from supportive care to disease-modifying therapies. Supportive treatment focuses on meticulous fluid management using loop diuretics and aldosterone antagonists, while avoiding beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and digoxin, which are poorly tolerated due to the restrictive physiology [21,22].

In AL amyloidosis, treatment is directed at eradicating the underlying clonal plasma cells. Current standard-of-care regimens combine the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib, alkylating agents, and dexamethasone with the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab, resulting in rapid hematologic and cardiac responses [23,24]. High-dose chemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation remains an option for eligible, lower-risk patients [25].

For ATTR amyloidosis, therapeutic strategies are divided into TTR stabilizers and TTR synthesis inhibitors. Tafamidis, a small molecule that binds to the thyroxine-binding sites of the TTR tetramer to prevent dissociation, was shown in the landmark ATTR-ACT trial to significantly reduce all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations in both ATTRwt and ATTRv patients [26,27]. TTR silencers, such as the small interfering RNA (siRNA) patisiran, or the antisense oligonucleotide inotersen, inhibit hepatic production of TTR [28]. These agents have demonstrated efficacy in halting or reversing polyneuropathy [29] and show promising results in reducing cardiac amyloid deposition and improving cardiovascular outcomes [30].

### Conclusion
Cardiac amyloidosis is no longer a terminal condition without therapeutic recourse. A heightened clinical awareness of red flags, combined with non-invasive diagnostic algorithms and novel, disease-modifying therapies, has shifted the clinical paradigm. Early diagnosis remains paramount to initiating targeted therapies before irreversible myocardial damage occurs.
